A cardioid is a heart-shaped curve traced by a point on the circumference of a circle rolling around another circle of the same radius. The name comes from the Greek word for heart. It's defined by parametric equations: x equals a times two cosine t minus cosine two t, and y equals a times two sine t minus sine two t, where a is the radius of the rolling circle and t is the angle of rotation. In polar form, it's simply r equals a times one plus cosine theta—one of the most elegant expressions for any polar curve. The cardioid has a single cusp, a sharp point at the origin where the rolling circle begins and ends its journey. It's a bounded curve, fitting entirely within a region determined by the rolling circle's radius. The area enclosed by the curve equals three pi a squared over two, or one and a half times the area of the generating circle. The cardioid appears in acoustics and antenna theory as the polar pattern of certain microphones and directional radiators.
